title: Query execution and planner
scopeHtml: Scope: EXPLAIN ANALYZE, scan and join algorithms, statistics, and common slow-query fixes. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: From SQL text to results: the pipeline
notes.html:
A query goes through parse, rewrite, plan, then execute. The parser checks syntax and names. The planner (optimizer) looks at many possible ways to run the query and picks the one with the lowest estimated cost. The executor runs that plan as a tree of nodes, each pulling rows from its children.

The planner is cost-based: it uses table statistics (row counts, value distributions) and cost constants (seq_page_cost 1.0, random_page_cost 4.0, cpu_tuple_cost 0.01 by default in Postgres) to estimate. Estimates can be wrong, and most slow queries are slow because of a wrong estimate or a missing index.

Worked example. SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7: candidate plans are a sequential scan, an index scan, or a bitmap scan. With 50M rows and an estimated 100 matches, the index plan costs maybe 20 units versus 800,000 for the scan, so it picks the index.

Industry examples. Postgres, MySQL 8, Oracle and SQL Server all use cost-based optimisers. Newer systems (CockroachDB, Spanner) use the same idea distributed. Google's and Meta's engineers have written about estimation errors being the number one cause of bad plans.

Everyday analogy. A GPS comparing routes using estimated traffic. If the traffic data is stale, it picks a bad route confidently.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking the database runs your joins in the order you wrote them.
  • Forgetting that estimates (not truth) drive the plan.

notes.title: Reading EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE
notes.html:
EXPLAIN shows the plan and estimates without running the query. EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs it and adds actual times and row counts. Beware: ANALYZE really executes (wrap INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE in BEGIN; ... ROLLBACK;).

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT c.name, sum(o.total)
FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.created >= '2025-05-01' GROUP BY c.name;
HashAggregate  (cost=2150.20..2160.20 rows=1000 width=40) (actual time=41.2..41.5 rows=980 loops=1)
  Group Key: c.name
  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 193kB
  Buffers: shared hit=1450
  ->  Hash Join  (cost=290.00..2000.00 rows=20000 width=36) (actual time=3.1..30.8 rows=21345 loops=1)
        Hash Cond: (o.customer_id = c.id)
        ->  Seq Scan on orders o  (cost=0.00..1500.00 rows=20000 width=8) (actual time=0.02..15.2 rows=21345 loops=1)
              Filter: (created >= '2025-05-01'::date)
              Rows Removed by Filter: 78655
        ->  Hash  (cost=165.00..165.00 rows=10000 width=36) (actual time=3.0..3.0 rows=10000 loops=1)
              Buckets: 16384  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 720kB
              ->  Seq Scan on customers c  (cost=0.00..165.00 rows=10000 width=36)
Planning Time: 0.4 ms
Execution Time: 42.0 ms

How to read it:

  • The tree is read bottom-up, innermost first. Indentation shows parents and children.
  • cost=a..b: a = startup cost (before first row), b = total cost, in arbitrary units.
  • rows= estimated vs actual ... rows= real. A big gap (10x or more) is the first thing to hunt.
  • loops=N: the node ran N times; actual time and rows are PER LOOP, so multiply. A nested loop inner side with loops=100000 is a typical culprit.
  • Buffers: shared hit (cache) vs read (disk); Rows Removed by Filter shows wasted work.
  • Planning Time vs Execution Time.

MySQL equivalent. EXPLAIN shows a table with type (ALL = full scan, index, range, ref, eq_ref, const), key (index used), rows (estimate), Extra (Using index, Using filesort, Using temporary). EXPLAIN ANALYZE exists in 8.0.18+ and prints a tree like Postgres.

Worked example (spotting the problem). Plan says rows=20 estimated but actual rows=2,000,000. The planner picked a nested loop because it expected 20 inner iterations; reality made it 2M. Fix the estimate (ANALYZE, extended statistics) rather than forcing the plan.

Everyday analogy. An itinerary with predicted and actual times for each leg: the leg where the two disagree most is where your trip went wrong.

Common interview traps.

  • Running EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a write without a rollback.
  • Ignoring loops.
  • Trusting cost numbers across different queries; they are only comparable within one planner.

notes.title: Scan types: seq, index, bitmap, index-only
notes.html:
The scan node says how rows are read from one table.

Node When it wins
Seq Scan Reading a large fraction of the table, or a tiny table
Index Scan Few rows, or needs index order (e.g. ORDER BY ... LIMIT)
Bitmap Index + Bitmap Heap Scan Medium number of rows: collects matching row locations, sorts them by page, reads each heap page once; can combine several indexes with AND/OR
Index Only Scan All needed columns are in the index (and visibility map is clean) 
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7 AND status = 'paid';
--  Bitmap Heap Scan on orders  (cost=12.4..560.0 rows=180 width=40) (actual time=0.15..0.9 rows=175 loops=1)
--    Recheck Cond: (customer_id = 7)
--    Filter: (status = 'paid'::text)
--    Heap Blocks: exact=160
--    ->  Bitmap Index Scan on orders_customer_idx (cost=0.0..12.3 rows=200) (actual rows=200)
--          Index Cond: (customer_id = 7)

Why bitmap exists. Plain index scans on 5,000 matches would do 5,000 random heap reads, maybe hitting the same page many times. A bitmap sorts page numbers first, reads each once in physical order (closer to sequential). Recheck Cond appears when the bitmap becomes lossy (work_mem too small, shown as lossy= blocks).

Parallel scans. Postgres can use Parallel Seq Scan with workers (max_parallel_workers_per_gather, default 2) for large scans; Gather merges results. Good for analytics; avoid in high-QPS OLTP where it steals CPU.

Worked example. A table with 10M rows (80k pages): Seq scan cost ~ 80,000 pages x 1.0 + 10M x 0.01 = 180,000. A filter returning 1,000 rows via index: ~ 1,000 x 4.0 random + overhead = ~4,000 to 5,000. Index wins by ~40x. At 3M matching rows the index would cost ~12M units, and seq scan wins.

Everyday analogy. Collecting 200 books: first write down all shelf locations, sort the list, then walk the library once rather than zigzagging for every book.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking Seq Scan is always bad.
  • Not knowing what a bitmap scan is for.
  • Forgetting ORDER BY ... LIMIT can make an index scan win even for many matches (stops early).

notes.title: Join algorithms: nested loop, hash, merge
notes.html:
Three ways to join two inputs. The planner chooses by estimated sizes, available indexes, and sort order.

Nested loop. For each row of the outer side, look up matches in the inner side. Great when the outer is small and the inner has an index; terrible when both are large with no index (O(n x m)).

for each row o in orders_filtered (outer, 20 rows):
    index lookup customers where id = o.customer_id      (inner, ~0.01 ms)

Hash join. Build a hash table from the smaller input, then scan the larger one probing it. Cost O(n + m). Needs memory (work_mem, default 4 MB per hash operation in Postgres); if the build side doesn't fit, it splits into batches written to disk (Batches: 8 in EXPLAIN). Only for equality joins.

Merge join. Sort both inputs on the join key (or use an index that is already sorted) and walk them in step. Cost O(n log n + m log m), or O(n + m) if already sorted. Handles huge inputs without big hash memory; supports range/equality on sortable keys.

Nested loop Hash Merge
Best for Few outer rows, indexed inner Big equality joins Pre-sorted big inputs
Memory Tiny Hash table of smaller side Sort buffers
Starts returning rows Immediately After build phase After sorts

Worked example. Join 10k customers to 10M orders on customer_id.

  • Nested loop (customers outer, index on orders): 10k x ~0.03 ms = 300 ms.
  • Hash join (hash 10k customers ~1 MB, scan 10M orders): ~1 to 2 s with cold data, less cached.
  • If the customer filter reduces to 5 rows: nested loop becomes 0.2 ms. The right choice flips with row counts, which is why accurate estimates matter.

MySQL differences. Before 8.0.18 MySQL had only nested loop variants (plus block nested loop). 8.0.18 added hash join (used when there is no usable index). No merge join. This is why older MySQL schemas had to index every join column.

Join order. For many tables, join order explodes (n! orders). Postgres searches exhaustively up to join_collapse_limit (default 8) and from_collapse_limit (8), then uses a genetic optimiser (geqo_threshold 12). A 12-way join can get a poor plan.

Everyday analogy. Matching names from two lists: look each name up one by one (nested loop), put one list in a hash/lookup board (hash), or sort both lists and walk them together (merge).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying hash join is always fastest.
  • Not knowing that a join can spill to disk when work_mem is too small.
  • Assuming the order you write the joins is the executed order.

notes.title: Statistics and cardinality estimation
notes.html:
Statistics are the numbers the planner uses to guess how many rows each step returns. Postgres collects them with ANALYZE (autovacuum runs it automatically) into pg_statistic, viewable via pg_stats.

Per column it stores: null fraction, number of distinct values (n_distinct), most common values and their frequencies, a histogram of the rest, and correlation with physical order. Sample size is default_statistics_target (default 100, meaning about 30,000 sampled rows per table via 300 x target).

SELECT attname, null_frac, n_distinct, most_common_vals, most_common_freqs
FROM pg_stats WHERE tablename = 'orders' AND attname = 'status';
-- status | 0 | 4 | {paid,refunded,pending,failed} | {0.9,0.05,0.04,0.01}

With status = 'pending' the planner estimates 0.04 x total rows. For 50M rows: 2M. Simple and usually right.

Where estimates go wrong.

  • Correlated columns. WHERE city = 'Pune' AND pincode = '411001': the planner assumes independence and multiplies selectivities, underestimating wildly. Fix: extended statistics: CREATE STATISTICS s (dependencies) ON city, pincode FROM addresses; ANALYZE addresses;
  • Stale stats after a bulk load: ANALYZE right after big loads or migrations.
  • Expression or function filters: no stats unless you create an expression index (which gets its own stats).
  • Skewed distributions with a big tail: raise the target for that column: ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN customer_id SET STATISTICS 1000; ANALYZE orders;
  • Joins across skewed keys.
  • Parameterised/prepared statements. After 5 executions Postgres may adopt a generic plan (plan_cache_mode auto) that ignores the specific parameter; a query that is fast for rare values and slow for the hot value (or vice versa) shows this; plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan can help.

Worked example. After loading 40M rows with COPY, autovacuum has not yet run; the planner thinks the table has 1,000 rows (old stats) and picks nested loops with seq scans inside. The query goes from 200 ms to 40 minutes. A manual ANALYZE fixes it in seconds. Metric to alert on: n_mod_since_analyze in pg_stat_user_tables.

MySQL. InnoDB uses persistent sampled statistics (innodb_stats_persistent, default on), refreshed by ANALYZE TABLE; MySQL 8 also supports histograms (ANALYZE TABLE t UPDATE HISTOGRAM ON col).

Industry examples. Postgres planner estimation blind spots (correlation) are a well-known cause of bad plans in production postmortems; teams respond with extended statistics, pg_hint_plan (an extension), or schema changes. Oracle and SQL Server give plan hints and adaptive plans more directly.

Everyday analogy. A survey sample used to estimate a city's population. A small, outdated or biased sample gives a confident wrong answer.

Common interview traps.

  • Telling someone to "force an index" before checking statistics.
  • Not running ANALYZE after bulk loads.
  • Ignoring column correlation.

notes.title: Common slow-query fixes
notes.html:
A debugging routine beats memorised tricks. Find the slow query (pg_stat_statements, slow query log, auto_explain), run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), find the node with the most time or biggest estimate gap, then pick the fix.

Fix catalogue:

  1. Seq scan on a big table with a selective filter: add the right (composite/partial) index.
  2. Function or cast on the column: rewrite the predicate or add an expression index.
  3. N+1 queries from the app: replace 1 + N queries with one join or WHERE id = ANY($1). 500 queries x 2 ms = 1 s of round trips versus one 5 ms query.
  4. Deep OFFSET: switch to keyset pagination.
  5. SELECT * on wide rows (large text/jsonb is TOASTed): select only needed columns to enable index-only scans and smaller transfers.
  6. Sort spilling to disk (Sort Method: external merge Disk: 120MB): add an index in the desired order, raise work_mem for that session, or reduce rows before sorting.
  7. Hash aggregate or join spilling: raise work_mem carefully (it is per operation per connection: 64 MB x 4 nodes x 200 connections = 51 GB).
  8. Correlated subquery run per row: rewrite as a join or EXISTS, ensure an index.
  9. COUNT(*) on large tables: Postgres has no free row count (MVCC); use estimates (reltuples), a maintained counter, or approximate; add filters + index-only scan.
  10. Lock waits, not CPU: EXPLAIN looks fine but the query waits; check pg_stat_activity.wait_event and pg_locks.
  11. Too many connections: use a pooler (PgBouncer); 500 connections cause context switching; target roughly 2 to 4 x CPU cores of active connections.

Example: sort spill.

Sort  (cost=...) (actual time=1850..2100 rows=2000000 loops=1)
  Sort Key: created DESC
  Sort Method: external merge  Disk: 187000kB

Fix: CREATE INDEX ON orders (created DESC) lets the plan read in order and apply LIMIT 50 after reading 50 rows (about 0.5 ms), removing the sort entirely.

Example: N+1.

-- App loop: 1 query for orders, then per order:  SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE order_id = $1;
-- One round trip instead:
SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE order_id = ANY ($1::int[]);

Worked example (production). An API endpoint p99 jumps from 80 ms to 4 s after a deploy. pg_stat_statements shows a new query dominating total_exec_time; the plan shows Nested Loop ... loops=250000 due to an underestimated join. After CREATE STATISTICS on the correlated columns and ANALYZE, the plan switches to a hash join: 90 ms.

Industry examples. GitHub, Shopify and Stripe engineering write-ups consistently find: missing/composite indexes, N+1 from ORMs, and stale/misleading statistics as the top three causes of slow queries. Tools: pg_stat_statements, auto_explain, pgBadger, MySQL performance_schema and slow query log with pt-query-digest.

Decision gravity. Query rewrites are reversible and local. Index and statistics changes are reversible but affect other queries. Query hints/plan forcing are fragile (data distribution changes); treat them as last resort and document them.

Everyday analogy. A mechanic: listen to where the noise is (measure), find the worn part (EXPLAIN), replace that one part (fix) and test-drive (re-measure) rather than replacing the whole engine.

Common interview traps.

  • Optimising without measuring or checking the actual plan.
  • Raising work_mem globally to a huge value.
  • Treating every slow query as an indexing problem (could be locks, N+1, connection storm, or stale stats).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Pipeline: parse, plan (cost-based, uses statistics), execute. Estimates drive plans.
  • EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS): read bottom-up, compare estimated vs actual rows, watch loops, Rows Removed by Filter, Buffers, and disk spills; wrap writes in a rolled-back transaction.
  • Scan nodes: seq, index, bitmap, index-only; each wins at a different selectivity.
  • Join algorithms: nested loop (small outer, indexed inner), hash (big equality, needs work_mem), merge (sorted inputs); MySQL got hash join only in 8.0.18.
  • Statistics: ANALYZE after bulk loads, extended statistics for correlated columns, higher STATISTICS target for skew; alert on stale stats.
  • Slow-query routine: find, EXPLAIN, locate the bad node, fix (index, rewrite, keyset pagination, N+1, spill, stats), re-measure.
  • Prefer the least invasive fix; avoid plan forcing and giant global work_mem.
